title: “Y” vs. “e”: What does “y” mean in Spanish?
summary: Spanish has two words for “and,” and you use them in different situations. Here are the rules about when to use “y” and when to use “e”!
body_markdown:
As Spanish learners know, the word for *and* is y


. You’ll see *y* almost as soon as you start studying Spanish, in phrases like café y pan


(coffee and bread), tú y yo


(you and I), and El búho es grande y me da miedo


(The owl is big and it scares me).


But as you learn more Spanish, you’ll find another way to say *and* : e


. *¿¿Y *y* e??* What’s going on here?


## When do you use *y* in Spanish?


In nearly all cases, *y* is the way you’ll say *and* in Spanish. Think of it as the default!


## When do you use *e* in Spanish?


There is one exception when it comes to *and* :


💡


If the next word starts with an “ee” sound, use **e** instead of **y** .


For example, if you want to describe a book as *fun and interesting* , you’ll use the word interesante


(interesting). Since the “i” of *interesante* is the same sound as the word *y* , you’ll use *e* before it to break up the sounds:


- El libro es divertido e interesante.


(The book is funny and interesting.)
- El libro es interesante y divertido.


(The book is interesting and funny.)


That’s the whole rule! Just the one exception, before words that also start with the “ee” sound. In addition to words that start with the letter “i,” like *interesante* , the rule also includes words that start with “hi,” like hijo


(son), because the “h” is silent in Spanish, and occasionally some words that have “y” as a vowel at the beginning, like the name Ysabel


.


For example, you’d say:


- padres e hijos


(fathers and sons), but hijos y padres


(sons and fathers)
- Pedro e Ysabel


(Pedro and Ysabel), but Ysabel y Pedro


(Ysabel and Pedro)


## Why does Spanish have two words for *and* ?


All languages have rules about[what sounds can go next to each other](https://blog.duolingo.com/why-is-pronunciation-hard/#sound-combination-rules-in-a-new-language) in words and sentences. In English, we have the rule that we don’t say *a* in front of words that start with a vowel. That’s why we say ***a** banana* but ***an** apple* . It’s just there to help hear when one word ends and the next one begins!


The same is true for Spanish *y* and *e* : In Spanish, you just don’t say y


before words that start with the “ee” sound! Instead, use e


.


## What about *o* and *u* ?


There’s a similar rule about the words for *or* in Spanish: The default word is o


, but when it comes before a word that starts with the “o” sound, like ocho


(eight), hombres


(men), or oro


(gold), you use u


instead. For example, you’d say:


- siete u ocho


(seven or eight), but ocho o nueve


(eight or nine)
- mujeres u hombres


(women or men), but hombres o mujeres


(men or women)
- plata u oro


(silver or gold), but oro o plata


(gold or silver)


## And… that’s all there is to it!


The rule for remembering when to use *y* and *e* (and *o* and *u* ) in Spanish is easy, but some patterns are trickier to learn. Keep practicing this and[other pronunciation rules](https://blog.duolingo.com/spanish-accent-marks/) , and over time these small differences will start to feel natural!
